pool.prompt: A GPON drop cable must navigate a 7.5 mm bend at a wall entry point. Which is the minimum ITU-T G.657 grade meeting this requirement?
choices: G.652.D — standard fiber handles most field bends
G.657.A1 — rated to 10 mm minimum; 7.5 mm is within this spec
G.657.A2 — rated to 7.5 mm minimum; exactly meets the requirement
G.657.B3 — only ultra-bend-insensitive handles 7.5 mm
pool.explanation: G.657.A2 is rated to a minimum bend radius of 7.5 mm — exactly meeting this requirement. G.657.A1 is rated to 10 mm and would not be sufficient at 7.5 mm. G.657.B3 (5 mm) would also work but is unnecessarily high-spec.

pool.prompt: A long-haul carrier hands off fiber at your CO. The splice record shows the incoming fiber is ITU-T G.655; your distribution plant uses G.652.D. What should you do before splicing directly?
choices: Splice directly — G.655 and G.652.D are fully interchangeable at the core level
Measure actual splice loss at the G.655/G.652.D interface — MFD differences may add measurable loss that needs to be budgeted
Replace the entire distribution plant with G.655 fiber for compatibility
G.655 is a multimode fiber — you cannot splice it to G.652.D single-mode
pool.explanation: G.655 (NZDSF) and G.652.D are both single-mode, but G.655 typically has a different MFD. Splicing them together may introduce measurable loss beyond a same-type splice — measure actual loss at the interface before finalizing the link budget.

pool.prompt: G.657.B3 fiber differs from G.657.A1 primarily in which way?
choices: B3 has a smaller physical core diameter (7 um vs. 9 um)
B3 is not guaranteed backward-compatible with G.652.D for zero-loss splicing due to potential MFD tolerance differences
B3 has higher attenuation at 1550 nm than G.657.A1
B3 cannot be used with GPON systems
pool.explanation: G.657.B3 uses a trench-assisted refractive index profile achieving very low bend loss but may have a slightly different MFD compared to G.652.D — it is NOT guaranteed backward-compatible with G.652.D for zero-loss splicing, unlike G.657.A1/A2.

pool.prompt: Match each installation scenario to the minimum G.657 fiber grade required.

items.label: OSP trunk cable on a gently curved aerial span (~200 mm bend)
FTTH drop cable with a 10 mm bend at a splice closure entry
GPON aerial drop with a 7.5 mm bend at a building wall entry
In-building MDU with 5 mm radius corners in tight cable tray

pool.explanation: Bend radius requirements scale with installation tightness: gentle aerial curves need no special bend-insensitivity, while progressively tighter bends (10mm, 7.5mm, 5mm) require the correspondingly rated G.657 sub-grade.

pool.prompt: Why is G.657.A1/A2 fully splice-compatible with G.652.D while G.657.B3 is not guaranteed to be?
choices: A1/A2 and G.652.D share the same MFD specification, so no intrinsic splice loss penalty occurs at the interface; B3's more aggressive trench-assisted design achieves lower bend loss at the cost of a potentially different MFD, introducing a splice-loss risk at a B3/G.652.D interface
There is no real difference — all G.657 sub-grades are equally compatible with G.652.D
A1/A2 are multimode while B3 is single-mode, making B3 inherently incompatible
Splice compatibility depends only on jacket color, not fiber grade
pool.explanation: G.657.A1/A2 were designed to maintain the same MFD as G.652.D, preserving splice compatibility. G.657.B3's more extreme bend-insensitivity (down to 5mm) uses a more aggressive index profile that can shift MFD away from G.652.D's value, creating a real (if often small) splice-loss risk that should be verified, not assumed.

pool.prompt: ITU-T G.655 is described as Non-Zero Dispersion-Shifted Single-Mode Fiber, engineered for long-haul DWDM. How does its typical chromatic dispersion at 1550 nm compare to G.652.D's ~17 ps/(nm*km)?
choices: G.655 has much higher dispersion (50+ ps/(nm*km)) to enable longer reach
G.655 has reduced dispersion (typically 1-10 ps/(nm*km)) to reduce four-wave mixing in DWDM systems while still allowing dispersion-compensating techniques
G.655 has zero dispersion at all wavelengths, unlike G.652.D
G.655 and G.652.D have identical dispersion profiles
pool.explanation: G.655's non-zero-dispersion-shifted design deliberately keeps some dispersion (typically 1-10 ps/(nm*km), lower than G.652.D's ~17) to suppress four-wave mixing in DWDM systems while still leaving enough dispersion for compensation techniques to work effectively.

pool.prompt: What is the primary use case for ITU-T G.656 (Wideband NZDSF), and why is it rarely specified for new builds?
choices: G.656 is the current default standard for all new OSP trunk cable

G.656 offers a wider low-dispersion passband (S-, C-, and L-bands, 1460-1625 nm) for metro/access WDM applications, but is now rarely seen in new builds — primarily encountered when reviewing legacy infrastructure
G.656 is exclusively for multimode data-center applications
G.656 was withdrawn by ITU-T and is no longer a valid standard
pool.explanation: G.656 was designed for wideband metro/access WDM applications with a low-dispersion passband spanning S-, C-, and L-bands. It's rarely chosen for new designs today, so a field engineer is more likely to encounter it when documenting or troubleshooting legacy infrastructure than when specifying new builds.

pool.prompt: What is the approximate minimum installation bend radius for standard G.652.D fiber, and how does it compare to G.657's bend-insensitive grades?
choices: ~30 mm for G.652.D — significantly larger (less tolerant of tight bends) than any G.657 sub-grade (5-10 mm)
G.652.D and all G.657 grades share the identical ~10 mm minimum bend radius
G.652.D has no minimum bend radius specification at all
G.652.D's minimum bend radius (30 mm) is actually smaller than G.657.A1's (10 mm)
pool.explanation: G.652.D's minimum installation bend radius is commonly cited around 30 mm across vendor/industry sources — meaningfully larger (i.e., less bend-tolerant) than G.657's specialized sub-grades (A1=10mm, A2=7.5mm, B3=5mm), which is precisely why G.657 was developed for tight-bend applications like FTTH drops and in-building routing. This ~30mm figure is an industry-convention rule of thumb rather than a single ITU-T G.652.D clause number; verify against the specific cable manufacturer's datasheet before design lock.
pool.citation: Industry-convention figure (vendor/FOA-style OSP installation guidance) for G.652.D minimum installation bend radius — not tied to a single ITU-T G.652.D clause; contrast with G.657 sub-grade radii (ITU-T G.657).
